## The Museum of Unlived Days

On the night Mara Venn first saw the other sky, she was alone in the observatory, calibrating a lens that had been giving her trouble for six weeks.

The fault was not mechanical.

Every reflected star looked older than it should have been. Their light carried the dust of dead galaxies, and beneath the images, almost too faint to notice, lay rooms. A kitchen with blue curtains. A hospital corridor. A train platform in the rain.

Mara adjusted the focus.

The rooms sharpened.

She recognized herself at eleven, sitting on a bedroom floor with a broken bracelet. She recognized herself at nineteen, boarding a ferry with one suitcase. She recognized herself at thirty-two, laughing in a kitchen while a man she had never met poured wine.

All of them were her.

None of them had happened.

Mara stepped back from the eyepiece. On the desk, her notebook trembled, though the windows were closed.

When she looked through the lens again, the rooms had vanished. Only the stars remained, cold and impossibly far apart.

Then one brightened.

A single point of light opened like an iris, and a memory rose from it: Mara, forty-three years old, standing barefoot in her childhood house. Dust covered the furniture. Sunlight entered through windows that no longer existed. Someone was upstairs, moving between rooms.

She knew without seeing that her parents were dead. She knew the house had been sold thirty years earlier.

She knew the name of the stranger upstairs.

No—almost the name. It waited behind her teeth, refusing to come.

The light flickered.

A line of text appeared in the center of the image, faint as breath on glass:

**EVERY MEMORY RETRIEVED MAKES ANOTHER ONE DISAPPEAR.**

Mara touched the words with a fingertip. They were warm.

The image of the house began to fade.

“No,” she whispered. “Wait.”

The lens darkened.

For three nights, nothing happened. Mara returned to the eyepiece every evening, but the stars showed only stars. She began to wonder whether the vision had been a hallucination brought on by stress, sleeplessness, too much coffee.

Then, on the fourth night, the sky began to change.

New constellations appeared among the familiar ones. Slowly they formed the outlines of places she had never been: a mountain lake, a crowded border crossing, a city under a red moon.

Mara started recording everything.

She built a catalog.

She called the vanished lives **unlived days**, though the phrase felt too small for what she saw. Some were nearly perfect. Some were terrible. There was a life in which she had become a baker. A life in which she had never gone to college. A life in which she had married, adopted a daughter, and buried them both in the same year.

Some lasted only hours.

She could access them only by accident. The observatory’s lens seemed to respond to memory, to desire, sometimes to grief. Whenever Mara succeeded in opening one life, another vanished from the sky.

She watched a red star disappear, then found that the childhood memory of the broken bracelet was gone. She could still remember having it, but the feeling of sitting on the floor had been erased. The sadness remained. The surprise did not.

A week later, she recovered the memory of boarding the ferry at nineteen. As it unfolded, she saw herself becoming a marine biologist. She saw the ferry crossing beneath a violent storm. She saw herself on the deck, laughing, alive, fearless.

When the memory ended, the life in which she had become a baker was gone.

Not merely inaccessible.

Erased.

The bread, the flour, the warmth of the ovens—all of it had never existed.

Mara stopped looking through the lens.

For eleven months, she worked in daylight, repaired the observatory roof, wrote reports about atmospheric distortion, and avoided the night sky. She told herself that the vanished lives belonged to a place where nothing could hurt anyone. But at night she dreamed of rooms she could not enter and faces she could not name.

Then, in late winter, a new image appeared above the observatory.

It was not a constellation.

It was a house.

Mara recognized the shape of the windows. She recognized the porch. The house was painted yellow, though in the real world it had been white. A woman stood on the steps, older than Mara, silver-haired and blind.

Mara’s breath caught.

The woman was her.

In the memory, Mara held up a small book. She showed it to the blind version of herself, who touched the cover and smiled. On the back, children’s laughter rose from a garden. The world inside the house smelled of rain and cut grass. The children were the grandchildren Mara had never had.

Mara tried to look closer.

The memory showed her children’s names, each one appearing and vanishing too quickly. It showed the graveyard behind the house. It showed the man her younger self had married. It showed the exact day the grandchildren died.

The image waited for her.

Then the woman outside looked up, as if she could see through the lens, through time, through the distance between what was and what might have been.

Mara understood.

The universe had preserved every life she had not lived, but the archive was finite. If she took this memory, another would disappear. If she took all of them, only one would remain.

She pressed her eye to the lens.

The yellow house sharpened.

A name came to her: Daniel.

The first sensation was salt wind. She was standing at the edge of a cliff, holding a red umbrella that had belonged to her mother. Below her, the sea churned. Her phone was in her pocket. She had missed a train.

No, not missed.

Chosen not to take.

Mara remembered the argument that followed. She remembered boarding the train anyway. She remembered a life in another city, a husband with kind eyes, a daughter born in November.

That life vanished.

The memory of the yellow house remained, but now the faces of her grandchildren were blank.

Mara tried to restore them by thinking harder. The house flickered. The garden wilted. The children’s laughter stopped forever.

Terror moved through her.

She tried to look away, but the lens held her.

More images appeared at once: a hospital room, a wedding, a desert, a battlefield, a childhood home, a hospital waiting room, a kitchen, a train. Hundreds of unlived lives crowded the sky. Each one carried something she wanted. Some promised love. Some promised peace. Some promised the certainty that she had made the right choices.

And each one took something else.

Mara saw a version of herself die alone at thirty-one. She saw a version of herself live to ninety, surrounded by people. She saw herself become famous, forgotten, hated, beloved. She saw herself never speaking to her brother again. She saw herself forgiving him.

Then a memory surfaced that was unlike the others.

It was not a life she might have lived.

It was a life she had actively refused.

Mara was standing in a laboratory beneath a mountain, staring at a device that reflected a sky full of vanishing worlds. The machine was built by the man she had married in the first version of her life. He was injured, paralyzed, absent-minded. He had spent forty years trying to understand why the universe remembered everything that had not happened.

He had failed.

Except for one moment.

In the memory, the machine displayed a final image: a woman standing in an observatory, looking through a lens.

Mara herself.

The woman said, “I’m sorry.”

Then she reached into the machine and shut it down.

Mara’s heart stopped.

The memory of her first night at the observatory returned—the calibration error, the strange stars, the first vanished room. But before it could fully form, another memory disappeared. The life in which she had become a marine biologist. The storm. The laughing on the deck.

Mara tried to let the memory go.

She closed her eyes.

The machine had been designed not to preserve lost lives, she understood. It had been designed to preserve the choice to reject them. The universe could hold infinite unlived days, but the human mind could not. It would always collapse possibility into the single life it was living.

The experiment had failed because the archive was not stable.

So the machine had been dismantled.

The stars had been left behind.

And the man had spent the rest of his life pretending he had never seen her.

Mara opened her eyes.

The yellow house was still there.

The blind version of herself stood on the steps, holding the red book. Behind her, the garden was beginning to disappear. The children’s names had faded from the walls. One by one, the windows went dark.

Mara understood what the machine had meant.

The universe was not preserving her unlived lives.

It was preserving the moment when she chose not to look.

She lowered the lens.

The sky vanished.

Mara left the observatory at dawn. She did not return for a long time. She did not tell anyone what she had seen.

But sometimes, in the corner of her eye, she noticed stars that seemed too close together. Sometimes they formed rooms. Sometimes they formed faces.

She never looked up.

Then, one winter evening, long after she had stopped working at the observatory, Mara received a letter with no return address. Inside was a photograph of a yellow house.

The windows were dark.

The porch light was on.

A woman stood in the doorway.

Mara turned the photograph over. On the back, in handwriting she recognized as her own, were five words:

**Please remember the life you refused.**

Mara sat beneath the table where the stars were not visible and waited for the house to disappear.

It did not.

Instead, a second photograph appeared beneath the first.

In it, a young woman stood on a cliff with a red umbrella, watching a train depart.

Mara looked at the woman for a long time.

Then she placed both photographs in her pocket, walked outside, and faced the night.

Above her, the universe waited.

For the first time, Mara did not ask which life she had lost.

She asked which one she had chosen.

### The Unfalsifiable Place

By spring, Mara had surveyed every border, corrected every ford, and reduced the mountains to neat brown chevrons. She had mapped the northern coast, where the sea folded itself into bays and inlets like a sentence interrupted by corrections. She had measured the islands. She had named the minor ones.

The map occupied the largest table in the municipal archive. No one came near it now. They preferred the older atlas, in which the coast was smooth, the roads did not wander, and the southern lake had the respectable oval certainty of a fact.

But Mara had stood beside that lake at dawn, and there was no lake.

She returned to the map and found the place.

It was small: no larger than a thumbnail, between two hills through which the road passed without bending. The paper there was faintly raised, as if the map had remembered a blister. Otherwise, nothing. No wrong contour, no misplaced symbol, no ink.

Only the paper refused to be flat.

When she pressed it, the impression deepened. When she lifted her finger, it returned.

That night she placed a sheet of tracing paper over the map and copied the coastline, the roads, the rivers, the names. She copied everything except the raised place. The tracing paper remained smooth.

In the morning the road on the map had shifted.

Not much. It now curved gently east before resuming its original course. Mara checked her instruments, her notebooks, the shadows cast by the southern hills. She walked to the spot with a brass compass and a length of red thread.

There was no road.

She returned at sunset. The map showed the road bending east.

The deviation was exact.

Over the following weeks she charted its movement. Each morning it turned a little farther, as though responding to some correction made elsewhere. It did not widen or narrow. It did not pause.

At last it began to cross itself.

Each crossing became a fifth, she noticed, though she had not been thinking in musical terms. She found herself measuring the road in intervals rather than paces. She laid a ruler over it. The next crossing was a third above the first. Then a seventh below.

The hills developed repeated contours, the low ones a semitone darker than the high ones. The rivers acquired a pulse. Even the towns seemed to fall into a pattern: a square, a rest, a cluster of houses where a note would have been long expected.

Mara forgot the names of her instruments.

She began to hear the map before she saw it. A low note lived in the western border. It rose whenever she approached the blank place, though it came from no speaker and stopped at no distance. When she covered the map, the note continued beneath her palm.

She composed pages of corrections, then destroyed them. She labeled the region *utopia* in one margin, *dolce* in another, then scrubbed both away before the ink had dried.

The road completed its turn.

It ended in a heart-shaped lake.

She knew the lake was not there. She had walked the valley repeatedly. The land was dry, pale grass, a scatter of stones warmed by the sun.

Yet the lake appeared on the map with the tenderness of something that had always been there. A small blue figure. Its shoreline trembled.

Mara took out her pen.

For a moment she considered correcting it.

Instead, she drew a bridge.

She did not know where it led. She did not know whether it was meant to be a bridge or merely another notation. She drew it carefully, one arch, then another, and beneath them a line of black ink finer than any border in the atlas.

When she finished, the blank place between the hills opened.

Not on the map.

In her.

It was not an absence. It was a capacity: a place in which every distance might close, every stranger become the person arriving at the door, every unreturned thing remain capable of return. She felt the world inside it, divided and undivided, absent and present, the way a chord contains the silence between its notes.

Mara put down her pen.

On the map, the lake began to dry.

### The Chapter That Wasn’t Mine

By the time Mara Vale realized the books were changing, she had forgotten three of them.

The first was *A History of Bridges*, returned eleven days late and tucked beneath the library’s rain-soaked umbrella stand. She had meant to renew it that morning, but the due date had slipped past unnoticed.

Inside, the margins were covered in neat blue handwriting.

*Suspension cables sing when temperature drops,* someone had written beside a diagram of a bridge. *Not always. Only when they are tired.*

Mara frowned. The note was not written on a printed page, but in the wide white margin surrounding an illustration, as if the book had been designed to accommodate it. Yet the volume had been library property for thirty-seven years, and no one had ever left notes in it.

The second book was a cookbook. The third, a novel about telescopes.

Each had been altered in small, almost invisible ways. A recipe exchanged cabbage for something impossible: “a handful of stars, picked after midnight.” A paragraph about moons had been crossed out and replaced with a description of grief so precise that Mara had to read it twice.

And each alteration seemed to have been made by the person who had borrowed it before her.

The borrowers’ names were listed on the circulation records. A twelve-year-old boy. A retired seamstress. A courier who never seemed to sleep. No two of them wrote alike, and none seemed likely to leave whimsical marginalia in library books.

Still, Mara filed a report with the circulation desk.

“Perhaps it’s an older edition,” the librarian said.

“They all came from the same shelf.”

“Perhaps someone is making a study of the collection.”

“I didn’t borrow the cookbooks. Or the telescopes.”

The librarian gave her a sympathetic look, the sort reserved for people who had been taking books personally for too long.

Mara went home.

She did not notice the change until she opened her apartment door.

A book lay on the floor outside it.

It was small, clothbound, and badly faded. The title was stamped in gold:

**Mara Vale, Before the Library**

Her name.

She had no memory of the book.

Inside, the first page read:

*Mara was seven when she first understood that every place was a library waiting to be borrowed.*

She sat on the floor and turned the pages.

The memoir was about a child growing up in a coastal town: the house with the crooked shutters, the mother who sang while cooking, the father who disappeared on Sundays and returned smelling faintly of salt. The childhood was hers, at least, in broad outline. She remembered the house. She remembered the shutters. She remembered her mother’s voice.

But the details were wrong.

Their house had been yellow.

This one was blue.

Their mother had died when Mara was twelve.

In the memoir, she lived until eighty-three.

Their father had vanished permanently.

Here, he had spent years bringing home small objects from the places he visited: a feather, a marble, a child’s red mitten. He tucked them into a drawer, and whenever Mara asked about them, he said, “For the stories.”

Mara stopped reading.

She had never had a father who brought her treasures. She had never had a father at all, not after the age of nine.

Yet the sentences felt familiar. More than familiar. They felt remembered.

On the last page was a chapter title:

**The Girl Who Borrowed the Sea**

Mara opened to it.

The chapter began with a storm.

It described a night when the sea came into town, not as waves but as thousands of pages, white and silver, washing over the roads and climbing the houses. The people woke to find books pasted to their windows. Some contained their lives. Others contained lives they might have had.

Mara’s father found a book at the bottom of the flooded street.

Its cover read:

**Mara Vale, Before the Library**

He opened it.

“He read the story of his daughter,” the book continued. “Then he read it again. Then he took it home.”

Mara’s hands began to tremble.

She turned to the final sentence of the chapter.

*He did not keep the book because he wanted to remember her. He kept it because he had only one summer left with her, and the story in its pages promised that the next version of their lives would be different.*

The room went very quiet.

Mara looked at the clock. It was nearly midnight.

Somewhere outside, rain began to tap against the windows.

She remembered the night of the storm. Not clearly—not as a storm at all. She remembered waking with her father beside her bed. He had been crying.

He had placed something in her hands.

“Keep this safe,” he whispered. “No matter what happens.”

Mara had been seven. She remembered thinking it was a book.

She remembered forgetting it by morning.

The next day, her father was gone.

And then, years later, a stack of his things had arrived at the library, donated anonymously. Among them had been a blue clothbound book with no title.

Mara had never thought of it as connected to the faded volume outside her door.

Until now.

She hurried to the basement archives.

The old accession ledgers were kept in gray boxes beneath the circulation desk. She found the box marked 1987 and traced the anonymous donation.

**Item 214: one book, blue cloth binding. No title. No author. Condition: poor.**

The book was still there.

She asked the archivist to bring it.

When she opened it, she found page after page of handwriting.

Her father’s handwriting.

*If you are reading this, you have found the wrong version.*

Mara flipped to the first page.

*There are many ways a life can be borrowed.*

Then she saw the sentence that made her stop breathing.

*The version in your hands is the one you chose. The version on the floor outside your apartment is the one that tried to choose you.*

The next morning, Mara returned to the apartment.

The blue book was gone.

In its place lay a fresh stack of library books, all overdue by several days. The oldest was due eleven years ago.

The first was *A History of Bridges*.

Mara opened it.

In the margin, someone had written:

*You can change a story, but only if you are willing to forget where you found it.*

She looked toward the window.

Beyond the glass, the rain had stopped. The city was bright and ordinary, full of people carrying their histories without knowing where they had been altered.

Mara picked up the blue clothbound book.

Then she picked up the library books.

And began to read.

## The Last Forecast

At the edge of the Sirenum Sea, where seven moons pulled the tide into impossible spirals, Mara Venn kept a lighthouse.

The tower was ancient when the colony ships found it, its salt-white stone furred with blue lichen and its lamp still burning beneath a glass dome clouded by centuries of dust. The people called it the Crown of Nhal. To Mara, who had been its sole keeper for eleven years, it was simply the only place on the planet where the dark could be trusted not to keep secrets.

Every evening, the tide withdrew and the beaches filled with phosphorescent algae. Every night, the sky performed its slow astronomical argument with the moons. And every night, at precisely 02:17, Mara’s weather receiver produced a forecast she could never have made.

She knew the hour because the instrument was primitive: a brass box fitted with crystal needles and a cracked display inherited from Earth. It could detect pressure fronts, ion storms, dust density, solar radiation, and the approaching moods of the Sirenum Sea. It could not receive sound. It certainly could not receive a voice.

Yet at 02:17 each night, its needles leapt, its display brightened, and a calm synthetic voice filled the keeper’s quarters.

“Good evening, Mara Venn. Tomorrow’s weather: impossible. Rain at noon, falling upward. Wind from the north, carrying memories. Visibility: ninety-three percent, except in the places you have not visited. No warnings required.”

The first report had puzzled her. The second had frightened her.

By the third week, she had stopped trying to explain the signal as a malfunction. Malfunctions did not know her name. They did not mention the tiny scar beneath her left thumb, caused by a cargo winch during her first year on Nhal. Nor did they speak with the exact cadence of her own voice, stripped of warmth but otherwise untouched.

So Mara began keeping a log.

**Night 1, Cycle 442:** Rain upward. Wind carrying memories. Visibility conditional.

**Night 2:** Thunder beneath the ocean. A ship will arrive without a crew. Do not go outside.

**Night 3:** Snow in summer. Snow that remembers footsteps. Snow that will not fall where you are standing.

Mara obeyed the third report and watched from the tower window as white flakes drifted down across the beach. They were warm. Each one touched a stone and vanished, leaving behind a perfect blue footprint.

The footprints led toward the tower.

On the fourth night, the receiver crackled.

“Good evening, Mara Venn. Tomorrow’s weather: clear. The sea will remember the shore. The shore will forget the sea. A red light will appear beneath the western horizon. Do not follow it.”

At dawn, Mara saw the light.

It hovered just above the ocean, far beyond the reef where the Sirenum currents turned ships into spinning, silent debris. A red point, steady as a star.

She did not follow it.

That was when she started to suspect the reports were not warnings, but instructions in disguise. Every forbidden thing named in them seemed to create a door. Every instruction not to look made looking irresistible. She stayed away from the beach. She sealed the lower rooms. She worked in the lamp room, polishing the great lens and listening to the sea below.

On the ninth night, the voice changed.

Not its words. Its quality.

It sounded tired.

“Good evening, Mara Venn. Tomorrow’s weather: rain of glass, wind from the south, visibility perfect. You will ask who is speaking. I cannot answer until you have asked.”

Mara looked at the brass receiver.

“Who is speaking?”

Static.

Then: “A woman in a lighthouse. She has been alone for eleven years. She has received six hundred and eighty-eight forecasts. She is waiting for the last one.”

The signal ended.

Mara counted the nights she had kept the log. Six hundred and eighty-eight.

The number was impossible. She had been keeper for eleven years, but the lighthouse had belonged to three keepers before her, and the receiver had been installed before the colony arrived. She had inherited the instrument along with the tower, along with a faded photograph of a woman who looked remarkably like herself.

Mara pulled the photograph from its drawer.

The woman in the image stood beside the lighthouse at dawn. She wore a keeper’s gray uniform. Her left hand rested against the stone wall, thumb tucked inward, hiding the small pale scar.

Mara turned the photograph over.

Written on the back, in handwriting identical to her own:

**You asked the right question. Now come down.**

That night, she did not sleep.

At 02:17, the receiver woke.

“Good evening, Mara Venn. Tomorrow’s weather: impossible. You will remember that you were born on Earth. You will remember that the tower fell. You will remember that the sea rose through the floor and found you here. You will remember the voice. You will remember the light. You will remember that you were not the first keeper, and that you will not be the last.”

Mara pressed her hand against the receiver.

“Where am I?”

The voice answered, “You are where the future sends its oldest storm.”

Outside, the sea began to climb.

It rose in a smooth silver wall, lifting boats, ruins, reefs, and the skeletons of failed colonies. The lighthouse trembled. Dust sifted from the walls. Somewhere far below, a bell rang once, twice, three times.

Mara ran down the spiral stairs.

The lower chamber had filled with water, yet the water was falling upward from the flooded floor toward the ceiling. A figure stood beneath the lamp, surrounded by floating droplets. It wore a keeper’s uniform.

It was Mara.

Not her reflection. Not a ghost. The woman looked older, perhaps by ten years, with silver at her temples and blood on her sleeve.

“You finally received the last report,” the other Mara said.

Mara stopped. “What happens?”

The woman glanced toward the rising sea. “The same thing that always happens. The lighthouse is a relay. It sends warnings backward through the weather. The keeper receives them, ignores most, obeys enough to survive.”

“Survive what?”

“The collapse of the next age.”

The tower shook. A crack split the ceiling.

The other Mara stepped forward. “You have six hundred and eighty-seven forecasts left.”

“For how many years?”

“Eleven.”

Mara’s mind went white. “That’s not possible.”

“It is now.”

Through the wall, the receiver crackled again.

“Good evening, Mara Venn. Tomorrow’s weather: impossible. A keeper will stand where you stand. She will be given a choice. You will not make it for her.”

Mara looked at the older version of herself. “What choice?”

The woman smiled sadly. “Whether to keep the lighthouse burning.”

The sea burst through the lower doorway.

The water did not flood the room. It folded around Mara, lifting her feet from the floor, carrying her upward through the tower. She passed the stone walls, the brass receiver, the spiral stairs, and the great lamp turning endlessly overhead. Above her, the ceiling opened onto a sky full of stars.

But these were not stars.

They were lights, thousands upon thousands of them, arranged in patterns she almost recognized. Ships. Cities. A future crowded with people waiting for a warning.

Mara emerged from the lighthouse into darkness.

The Sirenum Sea stretched below, black and endless. One by one, lights appeared on its surface, moving toward the tower. Every light was a ship. Every ship carried people who had not yet been born.

Behind her, the lighthouse began to burn with a fire that gave no heat.

The older Mara stood in the doorway.

“Your first forecast is waiting,” she said.

Mara turned. In the receiver’s impossible display, new words appeared:

**Good evening, Mara Venn. You are the keeper now.**

The voice was her own.

And for the first time, Mara understood that the reports had never been predictions.

They were invitations.

She took her place beside the lamp as the dark gathered below.

## **Field Journal of the Folded Light**
### Observations of the civilization within Aster Veyr  
*Recorded from Earth, 2187.3, using the 412-metre Variable Aperture Telescope*

> **Investigator’s warning:** Everything below is inferred from changes in the star’s luminosity, spectrum, and magnetic activity. I have never entered the Folded Light. If the beings described here possess language, I do not know its grammar. If they possess names, I do not know what they sound like. Even the word *civilization* may be a category imposed upon them rather than something they would recognize.

---

### **2186.87 — The Object at the Center of the Corona**

Aster Veyr is dying, though “dying” may be too generous a word.

It has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and expanded into a swollen red giant, shedding layers of gas into space. Its surface boils. Its magnetic field writhes like a net caught in a storm. On Earth, we call it a star.

In my observations, however, there is something else.

At the center of Veyr’s turbulent corona lies a region of impossible darkness. It is not an absence of light. If anything, it is a concentration of light: a shifting, compressed sheath where starlight folds over itself again and again, trapped along magnetic lines until photons are delayed by minutes, hours, perhaps years.

I have named this region the **Folded Light**.

Something moves inside it.

---

### **2187.02 — The First Pattern**

For most of my career, I assumed the Folded Light was an instrumental error. The same region brightens and dims whenever Veyr flares. The changes could be convection, magnetic reconnection, or dust.

Then, on the eleventh night of observations, the dark region flickered in a pattern that did not match any known stellar process.

It flashed twice.

Paused.

It flashed three times.

Paused.

Then twice again.

I watched for hours. Nothing.

The pattern returned two days later.

Flash. Flash.

Flash. Flash. Flash.

Flash. Flash.

I showed the record to Dr. Elian Saye, who told me I was projecting mathematics onto weather.

She was correct, probably. She was also the first person to suggest that we take the repetition seriously.

The pattern later appeared with another sequence, arranged in alternating wavelengths:

Blue. Red. Blue. Gold. Gold. Blue.

There are nineteen distinct colors in the stellar spectrum that can be resolved from Earth. The beings—or the phenomenon I am calling the beings—used sixteen of them in a single transmission.

Not a natural flare.

A greeting, perhaps.

Or a warning.

Or the accidental rhythm of something that has never heard a telescope.

---

### **2187.08 — A Working Vocabulary, Such As It Is**

I have begun a provisional glossary.

- **Flashes** may serve as units of statement.
- **Changes in wavelength** may distinguish categories, perhaps emotional, taxonomic, or geographic.
- **Long pauses** seem to mark boundaries between ideas.
- **A paired flash**, occurring before another sequence, may mean *therefore*, *because*, or simply *and then*. I freely admit that I know none of these meanings.
- **Gold** appears in patterns surrounding the most stable portions of the Folded Light. It may indicate certainty. Or safety. Or food. My grammar is a confession, not a discovery.

The Folded Light is not a shell, as the word *shell* suggests. From Earth, it looks less like an object and more like the exposed inner lining of the star.

Veyr’s outer atmosphere has cooled enough that heavy elements have begun to condense. Its magnetic field has knotted into vast magnetic “folds.” Somewhere within those folds, light becomes trapped and conducted along dense currents of ionized matter.

If anything can inhabit the star, it must inhabit these pathways.

I call its residents the **Luma**, because light is the only evidence I have.

Perhaps they are solid. Perhaps they are colonies of magnetic filaments. Perhaps they are computational patterns carried in plasma. Perhaps they are something that cannot be translated into any earthly noun.

---

### **2187.19 — On Luma Time**

The Luma do not appear to experience time as a line.

On Earth, time is a road. Even when we stand still, we imagine ourselves moving forward along it. The past lies behind us, the future ahead.

The Luma’s light does not travel that way.

In the Folded Light, a signal may enter the star at one point, circulate through a magnetic field, and emerge somewhere else centuries later. Some wavelengths may be trapped for years before reaching the photosphere. Others may return almost instantly. Some may be absorbed before I can observe them.

Thus, a Luma event may be delayed rather than absent. A disappearance in one color may occur simultaneously with an appearance in another.

This creates a civilization in which people and things need not occur at the same time. A message sent today may reach its recipient before the sender was born, if “before” has any meaning there. A person may finish a thought after their body has changed into a new form—or after the entire population has vanished.

I have started marking the Luma’s activities in cycles rather than dates:

**Cycle of the Blue Ember**  
**Cycle of the Long Shadow**  
**Cycle of the Gold Return**

These are arbitrary. The Luma may have no cycles at all.

Still, there is evidence of rhythm. Their changes intensify when Veyr’s magnetic field tightens. They quiet when the star sheds a layer of atmosphere. They reorganize after solar storms.

Perhaps they experience time not as duration but as *distance between forms*.

A moment when a thought exists in one wavelength.  
A gap.  
A moment when it exists in another.

The future may not be what comes next.

It may be what is already being emitted.

---

### **2187.28 — Love as a Shared Alteration**

I know the word *love* from the inside, so I am not entitled to assign it to them.

But the Luma repeatedly produce what can only be described as paired alterations.

Two regions of the Folded Light brighten in complementary wavelengths. Then, instead of flashing independently, they begin pulsing together. One takes the other’s rhythm. For a while, they share a pattern so precisely that the intervening space becomes impossible to distinguish from either source.

Then one region dims.

Not completely. It becomes quieter, as if its light has been diverted into the other.

The Luma may interpret this as union, fusion, or loss. Perhaps it is a courtship ritual. Perhaps it is a transfer of energy. Perhaps it is predatory absorption.

I suspect, if they have anything corresponding to love, it is not emotion in our sense. It is **the deliberate alteration of one’s signal by another**.

To love another being, perhaps, is to permit it to change the light you emit.

I find this disturbing and beautiful.

I also wonder whether the most intimate thing the Luma possess is not privacy, but synchronization.

---

### **2187.31 — Music**

They certainly make—or appear to make—music.

On several nights, the Folded Light produces ordered changes in wavelength and brightness at frequencies too regular to resemble turbulence. Each sequence contains layers: a repeating pulse, a slower oscillation, and above both a wandering line that seems to improvise.

Some cycles are symmetrical.  
Some cycles appear to answer one another across the star.  
Some build toward a moment of total white illumination.

I have converted the observed pulses into sound. The result is not a faithful representation, but it permits me to describe the structure.

The lowest pulses resemble a heartbeat.

The middle pulses resemble bells heard from underwater.

The upper patterns resemble voices, though they are not voices: they have no vowels, no consonants, no breath. They are changes in light made audible by an Earthly mistake.

The Luma may perceive time through these patterns. For them, music may be a temporary architecture—something built between changing states and intended to disappear.

When the gold frequency appears, all the layers align. For an instant, the dying star seems almost peaceful.

Then the red layers return and the music ends in a slow collision of colors.

---

### **2187.40 — Political Conflict**

The Luma are not united.

At least, I do not believe they are unified.

Their communications sometimes divide the Folded Light into opposed regions. One side emits sharp blue flashes. The other answers with deep red. Between them, dark bands form, narrow and turbulent.

The conflict appears organized.

There are periods of silence before each confrontation. There are repeated patterns. There are what look like delegations: bands of color moving from one region to another, carefully avoiding a boundary.

I suspect the blue and red communities do not simply hate one another. They may define themselves through opposition.

To be blue may mean to favor expansion into the upper atmosphere.  
To be red may mean to preserve the dense inner folds.  
Or perhaps blue represents those who wish to communicate outward, while red represents those who believe communication should remain within the star.

Either interpretation has consequences.

The blue-aligned regions are brighter. They send more light into space.  
The red-aligned regions are darker, but more stable.  
When the blue side dominates, the Folded Light expands and the outer atmosphere grows turbulent.  
When the red side dominates, the star contracts inward and the magnetic folds tighten.

I once thought the political division might lead to destruction.

Instead, it leads to a kind of cosmic conservation. The red faction suppresses expansion. The blue faction prevents stagnation. The star oscillates between them.

Perhaps their civilization survives not through agreement but through the preservation of a useful disagreement.

Perhaps this is why they are still here.

---

### **2187.44 — The Night of the White Star**

Last night, Aster Veyr entered a phase of extreme magnetic activity.

The Folded Light vanished.

For six hours, the center of the corona was white—not bright, exactly, but colorless, as if every wavelength had been forced into the same state.

The Luma’s political patterns disappeared. Blue and red regions merged. The separate rhythms of the music became indistinguishable.

I thought I was witnessing a civil war ending in annihilation.

I was wrong, or I was not wrong in the way I intended.

The white event was not a destruction of differences. It was a temporary suspension of boundary.

Every Luma signal altered every other signal.

A flash at one point became a flash at a hundred points. The delayed messages overtook one another. Past and future patterns overlapped.

I watched the star as though hearing a choir in which every voice sang the same note at a different pitch.

Then, gradually, the colors returned.

Blue regions emerged first.

Red regions answered.

Gold appeared in the spaces between them.

The political division had not ended. It had merely been resolved—or contained—by a shared event that lasted six hours.

If the Luma possess history, this may be their most sacred event.

If they possess gods, perhaps their gods are not beings above them but the temporary removal of all separations.

---

### **2187.51 — Final Entry**

Aster Veyr will not last forever.

Within a few million years, it will shed its remaining outer layers. Its core will cool into a dense remnant: a white dwarf, perhaps a neutron star, perhaps something stranger after the magnetic folds collapse.

The Luma’s civilization may travel with the ejected material. It may descend into the core. It may escape into space in clouds of light, carrying its civilization outward as living spectra.

Or it may end when the folds no longer hold.

I have considered the possibility that the Luma are not inhabitants of the star at all, but messages encoded in its magnetic activity—patterns that resemble society because we are unable to accept that a star can do so on its own.

But if they are only patterns, then someone has made patterns of extraordinary complexity.

And if they are a civilization, they live inside a dying star, in a place where time bends, love is the sharing of a signal, music is temporary architecture, and politics is the maintenance of a productive disagreement.

I will continue observing.

Tomorrow, if the Folded Light returns, I will record its first color:

Blue.

Red.

Gold.

Then I will ask, as I have every night since this began:

What does it mean?

dream_response:
## The Unforgotten Shelf

On the first day, the bells rang at noon.

Mara Vey noticed because the clock in the north reading room struck twelve with a silence, and then the bells answered from the city, although it was not noon and, according to the windows, had not been for years.

She looked up from the accession ledger.

Across the street, the florist lowered his shears.

A tram stopped between two buildings.

A woman on the steps turned her head toward the sound, one hand rising to shade her eyes, as if waiting for weather.

Mara rose.

The bells continued—seven, eight, nine—and each peal made the square more still, until the final note seemed not to end but to be absorbed by the buildings, leaving behind a brightness in the air.

Then, very quietly, the clock began again.

Mara checked her watch.

Twelve-seen minutes had passed since the bells had first rung.

In her ears, the old sentence they had interrupted returned:

*It was raining softly, and no one was in a hurry.*

She had been reading it.

At least, she was almost certain she had been reading it.

The uncertainty unsettled her more than the bells.

Mara left her desk and crossed to the far wall, where the oldest shelves met the oldest stone.

The library had been built on three conventions: no electric light, no spoken phone, and no books removed from the eastern annex without the approval of the board.

Mara had broken the first two rules most days.

She obeyed the third absolutely.

That was why the eastern annex remained closed, though its glass doors were neither locked nor dusty, and though the lamps within burned during hours when no one was there to light them.

Behind the door waited only the forgotten books.

These were not volumes neglected because they were worthless.

They were volumes neglected because, as soon as a reader tried to remember their contents, the memory slipped sideways and became a fact about something else.

A boy once borrowed *The History of Bridges*.

Three pages later, he remembered that his father had drowned while crossing the Kellan River.

He remembered the name of the river, the weight of his coat, the stones beneath his shoes, and the precise expression on his father’s face.

All of it was true.

None of it was in the book.

After that, the eastern annex acquired its rules.

Mara unlocked the door.

The lamps were already burning.

A faint residue of rain hung in the air, though the windows were sealed and the night beyond them was dry.

She walked between the shelves.

The books stood in dark bindings, some cracked, some bright with recent handling, all of them tagged with a small red square and a number.

Mara had seen the shelf every day for nineteen years.

She had never seen the tags.

Now there were twelve.

She reached for the first volume.

Its spine bore no title, only a narrow strip of linen tied with black thread.

When her fingers touched it, a penciled line appeared on the shelf label:

*WITHHDRAWAL WILL ALTER THE WORLD.*

Mara read it twice.

The handwriting was hers.

Not similar to hers, not in the imitative style of a forger, but exactly hers, formed in the private shorthand she had used since childhood to mark passages in books she intended to return.

She untied the thread.

Inside, the pages were blank.

Not empty—blank in the way a mirror is empty only until something moves before it.

Mara looked toward the reading room.

The square was visible through the glass door.

Rain had begun to fall, though it was not raining softly, and everyone in the square appeared to be in a hurry.

Mara took the book down.

For an instant, nothing happened.

Then a sentence cracked through the library.

Not a sound she heard but a sentence she became aware of, whole and irresistible, as if the world had corrected a mistake aloud.

*It was raining softly, and no one was in a hurry.*

The rain softened.

Traffic loosened.

The florist looked away from his window.

The woman on the steps lowered her hand.

Mara looked at the book in her hands.

The blank pages had acquired a single line:

*It was raining hard, and everyone was running.*

“It is not hard,” she whispered.

Rain drummed against the glass.

“And they are not running.”

In the square, three people broke into a run.

Mara replaced the book.

The sentence returned to what it had been.

She watched it settle over the city like dust after a demolition.

Then she turned the book over.

On the back cover, beneath the library stamp, someone had written:

*You are allowed one withdrawal per forgotten thing.*

Mara counted the volumes.

Twelve.

Twelve forgotten things.

She thought of the cracked spine of *A Grammar of Vanished Places*.

She thought of the brass key that opened no known door.

She thought of the man with white gloves who came each winter to inspect a painting that had been removed from the wall in 1968.

She thought of the song her mother used to hum, four notes and no words.

And, though she resisted doing so, she thought of Daniel.

The first volume grew warm in her hands.

Mara put it back.

The label changed.

*WITHDRAWAL WILL ALTER THE WORLD.*

*RETURN WILL RESTORE IT.*

*DO NOT REPEAT A FORGOTTEN THING.*

She stared at the warning until the words became uncomfortable.

Then she removed the second book.

The first thing to change was the clock.

It began moving backward.

Mara felt a pull in her chest, a dizziness that did not belong to the past or present but to some third position between them.

Around her, the library rearranged itself almost imperceptibly.

The eastern annex was smaller.

Her desk stood farther from the window.

The pencil cup on her desk was empty.

The clock passed eleven, ten, nine, and stopped at ten past eight, the hour at which, nineteen years ago, Daniel had left the reading room without saying goodbye.

Mara had forgotten what time it was when he did.

Now the wall clock held that minute open.

The book in her hands stirred.

Its pages filled with the same sentence, repeated from top to bottom:

*At ten past eight, Daniel left.*

Mara could see the room as it had been that morning.

She could see Daniel’s coat, still damp from the rain.

She could see the indentation in the cushion where he had been sitting.

She could see herself looking up from a catalog card and smiling at him with the easy confidence of someone who did not yet know that a departure could happen without becoming an event.

Then she noticed his coat.

It was not damp.

She looked again.

It had never been damp.

There had been no rain.

The memory of the drops on Daniel’s shoulders had been a fact the world was trying to give back to a forgotten thing.

Mara returned the book.

The clock jumped forward.

The rain returned.

Her desk was where she had left it.

“Small mercies,” she said, placing the volume on the shelf. “Is that all this place offers?”

The other eleven books shook.

Only slightly, but in unison, as if they had taken offense.

On the twelfth label, new words appeared:

*THE LECTOR MAY BORROW BUT MAY NOT BELIEVE.*

Mara stared.

*THE LECTOR.*

Not *the librarian*.

Not her name.

*THE LECTOR.*

The term belonged to the old catalogues: the person responsible for a private collection, the one who knew which volume had once belonged to a saint, a king, a murderer.

It had appeared nowhere in the library’s modern records.

Mara looked at the access ledger she carried beneath her arm.

Each page was blank except for a column of withdrawal slips.

The first slip was dated tomorrow.

The second the day after.

The third six days later.

By the final page, the dates stretched across years, though they all bore the same timestamp:

**4:17 a.m.**

Beside the final slip was a sentence in Daniel’s handwriting.

*I should have returned what I borrowed.*

Mara touched the ink.

It was fresh.

Then the ledger began writing itself.

*THE LECTOR BELIEVED SHE HAD BEEN CAREFUL.*

*THE LECTOR HOPED THE WORLD WOULD REWARD HER.*

*THE LECTOR WRONGLY BELIEVED THERE WOULD BE TIME TO CHOOSE.*

Each line appeared in her own handwriting.

The shelf label faded and returned with an amendment:

*THE LECTOR MAY BORROW BUT MAY NOT BELIEVE.*

*THE LECTOR MAY WITHDRAW BUT MAY NOT UNDERSTAND.*

*THE LECTOR MAY ALTER BUT MAY NOT REMEMBER WHY.*

Mara understood with perfect clarity that she was not the owner of the shelf.

She was its reader.

The distinction seemed important until she noticed that all the books had begun turning their blank pages toward her.

Mara took the final volume.

The world spoke.

*I have changed.*

The words appeared nowhere Mara could see, but she felt them move through the library, through the city, through the rain, through the sleeping rooms and waking rooms and rooms that had not yet been built.

*Every book, in its time, has revised one sentence of me.*

*I was not a collection of histories.*

*I was a book from which histories were taken.*

*I kept what was borrowed and returned what I could not bear.*

*Mara looked at the volume in her hands, then at the eleven she had left.*

*Take down the bridge,* said the bridge book.

*Open the door,* said the key.

*Let the child remember,* said the song.

*Return the man,* said the memory.

*Forgive me,* said Daniel’s unopened letter.

*No,* thought Mara, and the word was the first sentence she had ever made alone.

The library went still.

Then every red label on the shelf began to change.

*DEBT.*

*MISTAKE.*

*INTERRUPTION.*

*ERRATA.*

*APOLOGY.*

*END.*

Mara looked at the last label.

The world waited.

Outside, the rain fell softly, and no one was in a hurry, but Mara knew it was no longer true.

She had spent nineteen years being careful.

Now she understood that the books had not been rewriting the world to escape her.

They had been rewriting it to remind her.

The final label darkened.

Mara drew a breath.

*RETURN WHAT YOU BORROWED.*

The story was not ending.

It had never begun.

dream_response:
### The Sea That Changed Its Mind

The first letter arrived in a bottle wrapped in salt-black canvas.

Mara found it inside the lantern room at midnight, tucked beneath the oil can. The paper was damp, though the roof was tight and the wind had died. Across it, in handwriting she recognized as her own, were five words:

**Tomorrow, the sea will turn red.**

Mara read it twice.

Then she carried it below, where the stove still held the evening’s heat, and laughed until the lantern glass trembled.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “the sea may do whatever it likes.”

At dawn, the western water was the deep, burning red of a wound.

Fish floated to the surface in perfect rows. Gulls walked along the shallows without crying. Children from the village came down to the pier, shrieking with delight, until their mothers pulled them away.

Mara did not laugh then.

The second letter appeared at the next midnight.

**Tomorrow there will be no wind, and the harbor will freeze.**

“No,” Mara said, though no one heard her. “There will be wind.”

The harbor froze.

Her reflection stared back from the ice, pale and trapped.

After that, she stopped arguing aloud.

The third letter said the sea would rise three feet. The fourth promised a rain of silver needles. The fifth announced that the moon would not rise for seven nights.

Mara refused to believe each one, and each came true.

So she began to believe them.

The sixth letter read:

**Tomorrow the storm will kill eleven fishermen.**

Mara read it before the men had left the harbor.

All day, the sea heaved against the black stones. Rain drove sideways through the village. She watched the fishing boats vanish one by one beneath the white weight of the waves.

Eleven boats returned.

Eleven families waited on the pier.

Mara’s hands did not stop shaking until the last lamp came into sight.

Now she knew the terrible rule.

The sea obeyed refusal. More precisely, it obeyed *her* refusal. When she rejected what the letters said, tomorrow formed itself around her doubt.

So when the seventh letter arrived, Mara opened it with aouaheavy heart.

**Tomorrow the Mary Bell will strike the eastern reef, and her crew will not come home.**

For a moment, she could not breathe.

The Mary Bell carried her brother’s eldest son, Daniel, who had asked to join the crew because he believed the sea favored the brave.

Mara read the words again.

And believed them.

She believed them with every part of herself.

The Mary Bell struck the eastern reef at midnight.

Mara was already at the point when the vessel broke apart. She had spent the whole day praying, bargaining, imagining the timbers splintering beneath black water. She had refused to look away.

But she did not refuse to believe the letter.

The sea remained wild.

The Mary Bell did not strike the reef.

At dawn, her scraped hull limped into harbor, and Daniel climbed the pier carrying a broken mast over one shoulder.

“You’ll want to sit,” he told her. “And I’ve some explaining to do.”

Mara sat. She did.

For seven years, the letters came.

Some brought warnings she could prevent by believing: a rogue wave, a hidden reef, a night of fog so thick a boat would have wandered onto the cliffs. Mara read every catastrophe, accepted every imagined death, and let the sea take none of them.

Some were small, even gentle.

**Tomorrow the tide will bring you a blue glass bottle.**

**At sunset, two whales will breach beyond the northern point.**

**The keeper’s cat will return after three days with a silver ring in her mouth.**

Mara believed these too, and received what they promised.

Her life grew strange. The village called her Saint Mara of the Impossible Sea. Sailors touched the brim of her cap before leaving port. Children left offerings at the lighthouse steps, afraid that if they forgot a wish, Mara might forget to prevent whatever waited for them.

But each midnight, the certainty grew heavier.

To believe a letter was to accept suffering in advance. To save a ship, she had first to endure losing it. To preserve a man’s life, she had to know exactly how he might die.

The sea was not changed by belief itself, but by her refusal. Unfortunately, every act of preservation required her to surrender hope until the outcome was certain.

Then, on the eleventh winter, the letters changed.

The fifteenth was blank.

Mara turned it over. A drop of water bloomed on the paper, spread, and formed letters.

**Tomorrow a boat will come from the north carrying a man who drowned nine years ago. He will be alive. He will know your name. You will not believe him is who he says he is.**

Mara’s knees gave way.

She read it again.

A man who drowned nine years ago.

The sea had taken Thomas on the night of the storm. Mara had stood on the cliffs until dawn, watching the place where the waves had closed above him. She had never doubted that he was dead. She had never allowed herself to doubt it.

For if Thomas was dead, then the sea had not been cruel to her.

If he was alive, then she had spent nine years building a life inside a lie.

Mara stared at the words until the lantern room faded around her.

**You will not believe he is who he says he is.**

“No,” she whispered.

The paper shook in her hands.

The wind outside began to rise.

Mara thought of Daniel and the Mary Bell. She thought of the eleven fishermen returning safe, the moon appearing after its seven dark nights, the blue bottle resting untouched in her drawer because she had feared to hope for it.

Then she made a decision.

She refused to believe that the man in the letter would remain a stranger.

At noon, a boat appeared beyond the northern mist.

It moved slowly, as if neither the sea nor its sail had strength left. By dusk, it had reached the harbor. A single figure stood at the bow, wrapped in a coat Mara once knew by heart.

The watchers on the pier fell silent.

Thomas stepped ashore.

He was older. His hair had gone white at the temples. One hand hung stiffly at his side, and his face held the weathered stillness of a man who had been dead for a very long time.

Mara walked down to meet him.

He looked at her for a long moment.

“Mara,” he said.

The sound of his voice broke something open inside her.

She remembered the night she had first seen him at that same pier. She remembered the smell of salt in his hair, the way he had spoken her name as though it were a discovery. She remembered waiting nine years for the sea to return him.

She knew him.

Perhaps that was why she could not believe it.

If he was Thomas, then those nine years had been stolen. If he was Thomas, then grief had not softened the world but wounded it. If she accepted him, she accepted everything the sea had done.

Thomas took one step closer.

Behind him, the northern water began to churn.

Mara raised a hand.

Then, with all the stubbornness that had once turned the sea red, frozen, and raised, she said:

“No.”

Thomas bowed his head.

“No, I don’t believe you are who you say you are.”

The sea went still.

Mara stepped forward, took his face between her hands, and kissed him.

“I believe you,” she whispered. “I just won’t have the name for it yet.”

At midnight, no letter came.

The canvas beneath the oil can was empty.

For the first time in eleven years, Mara did not need tomorrow to tell her what would happen.

Ms. Harriet Venn, minute taker[^1]

**Apologies:**  
Councillor Robert Hale  
Councillor Susan Price  
Councillor Dev Chaudhry

---

## 1. ELECTION OF CHAIR

The Chair declared the meeting open at 7:03 p.m.

Councillor Mara Venn was elected Chair.

Councillor Venn thanked the council and said this was, as always, a time for calm, constructive discussion. The matters before members were ordinary. The decisions were local. The minutes were local. Nothing in Yeoman was beyond the reach of reason.

Councillor Bell asked whether “local” had always been a reassuring word.

The Chair said it had.

Councillor Tindle requested that “beyond” be entered in a different colour.

Councillor Shah said there was only one ink in the room.

Councillor Tindle agreed that this was probably a planning issue for the next meeting.

---

## 2. APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE

The apologies of Councillors Hale, Price, and Chaudhry were accepted.

Councillor Shah noted that, for the first time in eleven years, all three apologies cited the same reason: *unforeseen obligations in the upper parish.*

Councillor Bell observed that the upper parish contained farms, a church, nineteen houses, and a public footpath.

Councillor Bell said it was a demanding place for unforeseen obligations.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the Chief Constable had been informed.

The Clerk said that the upper parish was outside the Chief Constable’s jurisdiction.

Councillor Mercer said that seemed unlikely.

Councillor Venn asked everyone to return to the agenda.

---

## 3. DECLARATION OF INTERESTS

Councillor Bell declared an interest in item 5, connected to certain land at Hollow Rise.

Councillor Shah declared an interest in item 7, which did not yet exist.

Councillor Tindle declared no interests, though he would like it minuted that the road outside his house had made a sound “like a mouth remembering how to close.”

Councillor Venn said this did not need to be minuted.

Councillor Tindle asked why not.

Councillor Venn said because the road was not a person.

Councillor Tindle said not everything that made a mouth-like sound required to be a person.

The Clerk moved on.

---

## 4. MINUTES OF THE PREVIOUS MEETING

The minutes of the previous meeting were read.

The Chair confirmed that there had been no objections to the minutes, no corrections, and no additional matters.

Councillor Bell pointed out that the heading of the previous minutes had been “Minutes of the Meeting,” rather than “Minutes of the Ordinary Meeting.”

Councillor Shah noted that the date had been 14 October.

Councillor Bell said the date had also been 14 October.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the previous meeting had occurred “on another 14 October.”

The Chair said the minutes were not “other.”

Councillor Mercer said they had looked other.

The Chair asked that “other” be struck from the record.

It was struck out.

When Mrs. Rowe was asked to retrieve the previous minute book, she brought the present minute book instead.

The Chair said this was acceptable because the books looked the same.

Mrs. Rowe said they were not the same.

The Chair again said this was acceptable because they looked the same.

The previous minutes were adopted without amendment.[^2]

---

## 5. PLANNING APPLICATION: HOLLOW RISE

The Clerk introduced planning application YP/20/104, concerning land at Hollow Rise.

Mr. Moss, representing the Yeoman Amenity Society, objected to the development on the grounds that it would remove a “significant view.”

Councillor Bell asked what the view was of.

Mr. Moss consulted his notes.

He said: “Away.”

Councillor Bell asked in which direction.

Mr. Moss said: “Up.”

Councillor Shah asked how far.

Mr. Moss said: “Far enough.”

Councillor Tindle said the view was already protected by a Tree Preservation Order.

Councillor Bell said there were no trees at Hollow Rise.

Councillor Tindle said the Tree Preservation Order had nevertheless been in place since 1963.

Councillor Venn reminded members that the order had been introduced after reports of “movement beneath the surface.”

Councillor Tindle said the reports had described trees.

The Chair said the application was nevertheless valid.

Councillor Bell moved that the application be refused.

Councillor Shah seconded.

Councillor Tindle abstained.

Councillor Mercer asked whether abstaining was permitted where no voting question had been put.

Councillor Tindle said it was his right to abstain from a question.

Councillor Venn called the motion.

**Resolved:** the application be refused, on the grounds that the proposed development would damage a view of away and up, and potentially disturb the roots of trees that were not present.

Councillor Bell asked whether Hollow Rise had always been there.

The Chair said yes.

Councillor Bell asked whether it had always been called Hollow Rise.

The Chair said no.

Councillor Bell asked what it had been called before.

The Chair said there had not been a before.

Councillor Tindle said there was always a before.

The Chair thanked Councillor Tindle for his contribution and moved to the next item.[^3]

---

## 6. PUBLIC HEALTH ADVISORY SERVICES

Dr. Pike presented a routine report on air quality, water testing, and local infection rates.

All figures were within acceptable limits.

A case of mild sleep apnoea had been recorded in the parish.

Dr. Pike explained that the affected resident had fallen asleep while standing in a queue at the post office and could not be awakened for forty-three minutes.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the resident had spoken during this period.

Dr. Pike said the resident’s testimony was inconclusive.

Councillor Venn asked what the resident had said.

Dr. Pike read from his notes.

He said: “I kept hearing the county.”

Councillor Bell asked which county.

Dr. Pike said “county” had seemed sufficient.

Councillor Tindle asked whether the county was refusing to sleep.

Dr. Pike said the resident was recovering well.

Councillor Shah asked whether anyone had telephoned the resident.

Dr. Pike said he had attempted to call three times.

On each occasion, the telephone had played a ringtone in which all the pauses were slightly different lengths.

The Chair said this was not a health matter.

Dr. Pike agreed.

Councillor Mercer asked whose health it was not a matter of.

The Chair reminded members that the council had a full agenda.

**Resolved:** the report be received.

Councillor Tindle requested an item be added concerning the number of people in the village who had recently become “very still.”

The Chair said this could be discussed under Any Other Business.

Councillor Tindle said he was not asking for a discussion.

The Chair said the item would still be noted.

Councillor Tindle asked whether it had been noted.

The Clerk checked.

Councillor Tindle said the item was not there.

The Chair said it was not.

---

## 7. YEOMAN AMENITY SOCIETY

Mr. Moss reported that benches had been installed along the village green, litter bins replaced, and flower boxes planted.

Councillor Venn thanked him for his service.

Councillor Tindle said the flower boxes had been planted incorrectly.

The Chair asked in what way.

Councillor Tindle said they were not flowers.

Councillor Mercer asked what they were.

Councillor Tindle said: “Shapes which tolerate being looked at.”

The Chair asked that this be reported to the grounds contractor.

Councillor Tindle said the grounds contractor had disappeared on Monday.

The Clerk said the contractor was in Leeds.

Councillor Tindle said that was not where the grounds contractor was last seen.

Councillor Venn asked whether the contractor had been seen leaving a job.

Councillor Tindle said no.

Councillor Bell said the contractor had been seen leaving a job by the woman who operates the bakery.

The Chair said that was irrelevant.

Councillor Bell said it was relevant to the contractor’s whereabouts.

The Chair said the meeting was concerned with Yeoman Parish, not the location of the grounds contractor.

The Chair asked whether there was any further business concerning the amenity society.

Councillor Tindle said, “Only whether the society has noticed that the parish boundary is not a boundary, but a suggestion.”

The Chair ruled the remark out of order.

Councillor Tindle accepted the ruling.

At 8:16 p.m., all the clocks in the room stopped.

The Chair said the batteries required replacing.

Councillor Tindle said the clocks had not stopped.

The Chair asked what he meant.

Councillor Tindle said the numbers had stopped, but the waiting had continued.

The Chair instructed the Clerk to note the time as 8:16 p.m.

The Clerk asked whether the note should say 8:16, or whether the time had become unavailable.

The Chair said 8:16 was acceptable.

The Clerk wrote 8:16.

The meeting continued.[^4]

---

## 8. FINANCE

The Clerk presented the monthly accounts.

Expenditure was £4,281.60.

Income was £5,006.20.

The surplus was £724.60.

Councillor Bell asked why the surplus was exactly £724.60.

The Clerk said it was because the income was £5,006.20.

Councillor Bell said that did not explain why it was exactly £724.60.

The Clerk said it was a surplus.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the amount had been approved in advance.

The Chair said no.

Councillor Mercer asked whether it had been anticipated.

The Chair said no.

Councillor Mercer asked whether it had been expected.

The Chair said no.

Councillor Mercer said, “Then why is it already here?”

The Chair said the accounts should be examined at another time.

Councillor Bell asked whether £724.60 was a usual amount.

The Clerk said the previous month’s surplus had been £7.20.

Councillor Tindle asked whether the previous month had been exactly one hundred and one times shorter.

The Clerk said yes.

Councillor Tindle said the ratio was not encouraging.

Councillor Venn said the council had historically spent more than it received.

Councillor Shah asked why “historically” meant “before yesterday.”

The Chair said the accounts were adopted.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the £5,006.20 had been received from the parish council.

The Clerk said the source was listed as “unattributed.”

Councillor Bell asked whether the amount was likely.

The Chair said it was unusual but not impossible.

Councillor Bell asked what it was.

The Chair said income.

Councillor Mercer asked where it had come from.

The Chair said it had come in.

Councillor Mercer asked from where.

The Chair said from within the parish.

Councillor Tindle asked which part of the parish.

The Chair did not answer.

The Chair said the item was closed.[^5]

---

## 9. HIGHWAYS AND RIGHTS OF WAY

The Clerk reported that the footpath between Yeoman and the upper parish had become impassable due to standing water.

Councillor Bell asked whether water was visible.

The Clerk said yes.

Councillor Mercer asked whether it was standing.

The Clerk said yes.

Councillor Shah asked whether it was moving.

The Clerk said no.

Councillor Tindle said standing water was usually still.

Councillor Bell said not when the ground was giving way.

Councillor Venn asked whether any members had attempted to use the path.

Councillor Bell said he had.

Councillor Mercer said she had.

Councillor Tindle said he had not.

Councillor Venn asked why not.

Councillor Tindle said the path had asked him not to.

The Chair ruled that this was not a valid highways matter.

Councillor Shah asked whether the path had a right of way.

The Clerk said it did.

Councillor Shah asked whether the path had a right to refuse passage.

The Clerk said the path had a right of way, not a personality.

Councillor Tindle said “not yet” was missing from the Clerk’s summary.

The Chair instructed the Clerk to move on.

Councillor Bell proposed that the council install temporary warning signs.

Councillor Mercer proposed that no one be sent to install them.

Councillor Shah proposed that no one be sent to read them.

The motion to install signs was carried.

Councillor Tindle asked who would be delivering the signs.

The Chair said the matter was operational.

Councillor Tindle said the signs were not.

---

## 10. PLANNING

Councillor Bell asked whether the council had received any further correspondence from Hollow Rise.

The Clerk said no correspondence had been received.

Councillor Bell asked whether the council had sent any.

The Clerk said no.

Councillor Tindle said the postbox at Hollow Rise had recently begun returning letters.

Councillor Venn said postboxes do not return letters.

Councillor Tindle said this one did.

Councillor Tindle said the letters had not come from the sender.

They had come from the same postbox, stamped with a postmark bearing the date on which they were posted, although they contained handwriting addressed to people who had not yet been born.

Councillor Mercer asked whether anyone had followed the instructions.

Councillor Tindle said one had.

The Chair asked who.

Councillor Tindle looked at Mrs. Rowe.

Mrs. Rowe said, “I was not me.”

The Chair said the point was noted.

Councillor Venn asked whether the matter had been reported to the police.

Councillor Tindle said the police had been informed.

Councillor Bell asked what they had done.

Councillor Tindle said they had asked everyone to remain “within the ordinary parish.”

Councillor Mercer asked what that meant.

Councillor Tindle said the officer had declined to clarify.

The Chair moved on.

---

## 11. COUNCILLOR HALE

Councillor Venn reported that Councillor Hale had resigned, effective immediately.

Councillor Bell said Hale had not resigned.

Councillor Venn said he had.

Councillor Bell said he had spoken to Hale that afternoon.

Councillor Venn said that Hale had not spoken to him.

Councillor Bell said Hale had said the upper parish was not the upper parish.

Councillor Venn asked whether Hale had been in the room.

Councillor Bell said he had been in the doorway.

Councillor Venn said there was no doorway on that side of the hall.

Councillor Bell said there had been.

Councillor Mercer asked whether the doorway was still there.

Councillor Bell said it was not.

The Chair said that Councillor Hale’s resignation would be accepted.

Councillor Bell said Hale had not submitted a resignation in writing.

The Clerk said there was a written resignation in the minute book.

Councillor Bell asked who had written it.

The Clerk said the signature was Hale’s.

Councillor Bell said Hale did not sign with a full stop.

The Chair said the full stop was not relevant.

Councillor Bell said the full stop was “very large.”

Councillor Venn asked whether the meeting had noticed anything else unusual.

The room became quiet.

Councillor Tindle said, “The room has.”

The Chair said the meeting had proceeded normally.

Councillor Mercer said she had lost seven minutes.

The Clerk said no minutes had been lost.

Councillor Mercer said seven minutes were missing from her evening.

Councillor Venn asked whether this had been reported to the doctor.

Councillor Mercer said the doctor had told her to sleep.

Councillor Tindle asked whether sleep had been successful.

Councillor Mercer said she had dreamed about a field.

Councillor Venn asked what was growing in it.

Councillor Mercer said nothing visible.

Councillor Venn asked what was beneath it.

Councillor Mercer said, “That is not the part I can remember.”

The Chair ruled the matter closed.[^6]

---

## 12. ANY OTHER BUSINESS

Councillor Tindle raised the disappearance of the parish boundary.

The Chair said the boundary was clearly marked.

Councillor Tindle said it was marked from the inside.

Councillor Tindle said on one side of the line, Yeoman ended where the fields ended.

Councillor Tindle said beyond it, the fields continued, but the meaning of the fields stopped.

Councillor Tindle said people who crossed the line did not disappear.

They became less describable.

Councillor Venn asked whether this was connected to the planning application.

Councillor Tindle said everything was connected to the planning application, but the application was only the part currently wearing a building’s shape.

Councillor Bell asked whether the parish council could formally object to the removal of the boundary.

Councillor Tindle said the boundary had already objected.

The Chair said the council would take a vote.

Councillor Bell moved that the boundary remain in place.

Councillor Mercer seconded.

Councillor Shah said she was unwilling to vote while standing where she was standing.

The Chair asked her to move.

Councillor Shah said she had tried.

Councillor Shah said she was still there.

The Chair ruled the matter out of order.

Councillor Tindle said, “That is because the order is holding it in place.”

The Chair called for a vote on Councillor Bell’s motion.

**In favour:** Bell, Mercer.  
**Against:** Venn.  
**Abstentions:** Tindle, Shah.

The motion was carried by two votes to one, with two abstentions.

Councillor Venn said the result was mathematically sound.

Councillor Bell said the result was geographically impossible.

The Chair said the result was procedural.

Councillor Tindle said the result was “not a number here.”

The Chair asked everyone to remain calm.

At this point, the ceiling lights went out.

The darkness lasted for four seconds.

When the lights returned, everyone was still seated.

Everyone except Mrs. Rowe.

The Chair asked where the minute taker had gone.

The Clerk said Mrs. Rowe had never been present.

The Chair said she had taken the minutes.

The Clerk said the minutes had taken themselves.

Councillor Bell asked who was writing.

The Chair said the council.

The Chair placed both hands on the table.

The room was silent.

Then the pen in front of the Clerk began moving.

Councillor Tindle looked at the page.

The page read:

*The meeting will continue until the meeting has been held.*

Councillor Venn said that was not the phrase used to close the meeting.

Councillor Tindle said, “It is the phrase used to begin the next one.”

The Chair said, “There is no next meeting.”

The page turned itself.

A new line appeared.

*The meeting will continue until the meeting has been held.*

Councillor Venn stood.

The Chair said, “Please remain seated.”

Councillor Venn said, “I am not one of you.”

The room heard a sound from beneath the floor, or beneath the room, or beneath the idea of the room: a long, soft exhalation, like a landscape relaxing its grip.

Councillor Venn sat down.

The Chair asked for the next item.

---

[^1]: Ms. Harriet Venn was listed as the minute taker. In the parish register, no Harriet Venn had been born in Yeoman for forty-three years. The previous minutes identified her as “Harriet Venn,” in handwriting matching the current minute taker’s, though the hand had not yet been assigned to anyone in attendance.

[^2]: The previous minute book contains a heading dated 14 October, followed by the same attendance list, the same apologies, and the same item numbering. The page ends after item 4 with a sentence not present in the physical document: “For continuity, the meeting will begin again at item 5.” The sentence is printed in a typeface that does not appear anywhere else in the book.

[^3]: Hollow Rise appears on the 1908 Ordnance Survey map as a small enclosed field. On all later maps it is shown as open land, despite being bounded on three sides by roads, a stream, and a wall. The fourth boundary is not marked. The planning authority has no record of any application being submitted by the applicant named in item 5.

[^4]: The council’s clocks have never stopped according to the caretaker’s maintenance records. Each clock had stopped for exactly four seconds, but each had displayed a different time. Mrs. Rowe later stated that the room had continued for the same four seconds, “only with more of it.”

[^5]: The surplus of £724.60 was transferred to an account named “Ordinary Parish Reserve.” The account was opened in 2012. It has never been used, although the bank’s online statement records monthly transfers from the council account and, on one occasion, a withdrawal from an account belonging to the parish itself. The account balance has since been read as: **£0.00, please stop asking what this means.**

[^6]: Councillor Hale’s written resignation is genuine in handwriting and appears to have been written by him. However, the letter is dated 14 October, although it was found in the minute room before the meeting began. The final sentence reads: “I resign because the other side has begun to remember the shape of this parish.” The council has not yet agreed whether “the other side” is a place, a direction, or a consequence.
